summary: Introduces a command set for web-based Network Looking Glass software, giving programmers uniform access and a standardized response, with the same information as the web interfaces.

plainLanguage.summary: Looking glass pages let you peek at a network. This gives programs the same buttons so they need no web page.

questions: what is a network looking glass
how do i query a looking glass programmatically
what commands does looking glass provide
subtitle: A standardized API for querying Network Looking Glass services.

tldr.problem: Network Looking Glass services let people check routing information and network paths, but each Looking Glass implementation has its own web interface, making it hard to automate queries or use multiple Looking Glasses together.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8522 defines a standard command set that Looking Glass services can implement, allowing clients to issue HTTP GET requests with parameters like 'ping', 'traceroute', and 'show route', and receive JSON responses in a standardized format.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now programmatically query Looking Glass services using the same commands across different ISP and IXP implementations, without needing to scrape web pages or maintain separate integrations for each service.

today: RFC 8522 is an Informational RFC that standardizes the Looking Glass command set. The specification has been registered with IANA as a Well-Known URI and provides a baseline that Looking Glass implementers can follow. Various network operators have adopted or implemented support for this standard, enabling automated, scriptable access to looking glass functionality across the Internet.

sections.title: Looking Glass Services
sections.content:
Many Internet service providers (ISPs) and Internet exchange points (IXPs) offer a web-based service that gives visibility into their backbone routing tables, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) peer information, and announced routes. This service is called a Network Looking Glass.

Each Looking Glass implementation has had its own web interface, making it difficult for programmers to automate access or switch between different implementations. RFC 8522 solves this by defining a common command set that multiple Looking Glass providers can implement, allowing applications to use Looking Glass services programmatically with a uniform interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks have windows you can look through to see their routing tables. But each window had different buttons. Now they all use the same buttons.

sections.title: How the Looking Glass API Works
sections.content:
Clients issue queries to the Looking Glass server using HTTP GET requests to the .well-known/looking-glass path. The client specifies the operation ('function') it wants executed on a selected router, and the server executes a corresponding command on that router.

The server responds with JSON in JSend format, containing a status field of 'success', 'fail', or 'error'. A successful response includes the performed time, runtime in seconds, the router name, and the output in the requested format (defaulting to raw text). Clients can request specific output formats like 'application/yang' or 'text/plain'.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a message asking the service to run a command on its router. It replies with the answer in a message envelope that says whether it worked and how long it took.

sections.title: Command Categories
sections.content:
Diagnostic commands are mandatory: 'ping' sends echo messages to test reachability and measure latency. Optional diagnostic commands include 'traceroute' to trace the path to a destination.

Informational commands provide visibility into the network: 'show route' retrieves routing table entries, 'show bgp' displays BGP routing information, 'show bgp summary' prints BGP neighbor status, and 'show bgp neighbors' provides detailed BGP connection details.

Organizational commands are mandatory: 'routers' lists available routers, 'routers/{id}' shows details about a specific router, and 'commands' lists all available commands. Implementers can add extensible commands for additional functionality, like OSPF commands in networks that use OSPF instead of BGP.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ping a server, trace routes to it, look up routing tables, check BGP status, and ask what commands are available. You pick which router to query.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
All operations are stateless and read-only; clients cannot execute arbitrary commands on routers. Parameters are case-insensitive. The command set uses URI templates following RFC 6570, making it extensible and language-independent. Any programming language that implements the commands is acceptable.

Protocol parameters specify which router to use (by name or index), the address family (IPv4, IPv6, or other), any virtual routing table (VRF), a runtime timeout (default 30 seconds), and output format preference. The response indicates which router executed the command and how long it took.
sections.plainLanguage: The API is simple: you ask for something, the server safely runs it on a router, and gives you back the answer in a standard format. You cannot break anything because you cannot change anything.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC requires HTTPS to ensure transit security and privacy. It acknowledges that scripted access to the Looking Glass API could be abused for Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, and recommends that implementers mitigate this through rate-limiting and IP-based blocking. Authentication is optional because current Looking Glass web services require none, but implementers may add authentication based on their security requirements.

Some Looking Glass commands provide detailed insight into the network, so implementers should use security policy to disable optional commands or restrict access where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Use HTTPS to keep it secret. Be careful not to let attackers abuse it for DDoS. You can restrict which commands people are allowed to run.
